name: MCP-Atlas
intro: MCP-Atlas 是一个面向生产级 MCP 工具使用的大规模基准，包含 36 个真实服务器、全部任务使用的 220 个工具和 1,000 个专家编写任务，并随机拆分为 500 题公开集与 500 题私有集。任务不泄露服务器、工具或参数，并加入语义相近干扰项；通过判定只取决于最终答案对原子事实声明的覆盖率。
build_method: 专家构建, 人工与自动质检
metric: 声明覆盖率, Pass@0.75, 通过率
eval_feature: 单轮任务, 多步工具交互, 结果导向, 动态真实端点
build_method_en: Expert Curation, Human and Automated QA
eval_feature_en: Single-turn Tasks, Multi-step Tool Interaction, Result-oriented, Dynamic Live Endpoints
intro_en: MCP-Atlas is a large-scale benchmark for production MCP tool use with 36 real servers, 220 tools used across its 1,000 expert-authored tasks, and a random 500-public / 500-private split. Prompts reveal no server, tool, or parameter names and include semantically plausible distractors; pass/fail depends only on final-answer coverage of atomic factual claims.

drawio_review_note: Paper-alignment review passed against arXiv:2602.00933v3 (2026-05-19), especially Sections 3.1-3.4 and the Limitations, Server and Tool Inventory, Evaluator Prompt, Confidence Intervals, Task Authoring Templates, Failure Mode Taxonomy, Cross-Judge Agreement, Access/Licensing/Reproducibility, and Formalization appendices. The versioned arXiv PDF is byte-identical to assets/MCP_Atlas.pdf at official Git commit b6edd44b69892894ffa282f356e2dba41b41e298 and has SHA-256 2cd00f60d5ac0324ee9edd8693a4a3be61dc3a06c550209310fbf7581917315d. The former preferred CloudFront PDF was a stale 20-page artifact with SHA-256 7910dc144b6319bae162c8e8089da3af6d5fcf455e2d689811d6837c30414600, so pdf_cdn_url now points to the versioned v3 PDF instead of shadowing it. The paper constructs 1,000 English single-turn tasks through paid expert authoring averaging 4.6 hours per task over 36 production MCP servers and 220 tools used across all tasks in five domains. Each prompt must be tool-dependent, stable, natural, and unambiguous; it hides server, tool, and parameter names. Each custom environment exposes 6-37 tools (mean 15.2), requires 2-8 (mean 4.1), and adds a mean 11.1 plausible distractors. Experts execute a minimal sufficient reference trajectory, author atomic claims grounded in returned evidence, and provide the task deliverables; the full set averages 4.7 claims (range 1-23). Reference trajectories support solvability checks, tool-dependence validation, and post-hoc diagnostics only and never constrain pass/fail, so alternative valid tool paths can earn full credit. Five QA layers are preserved exactly: expert reference execution, domain-expert correctness/solvability review, secondary prompt-leakage review, automated LLM checks of claim completeness and trajectory consistency, and random-sample manual audit. Tasks are randomly split 500 public / 500 private; the private half is absent from the release and is reserved for exposure monitoring and leaderboard integrity. Evaluation holds prompt, exposed tools, 100-tool-call budget, rubric, and final-answer protocol fixed at task level while permitting only provider-specific low-level adapters and no model-specific demonstrations, retries, prompts, or scaffolding. The model interacts with real endpoints and emits a final text answer; reaching 100 calls still permits partial-response grading. The primary evaluator is Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview and is invoked independently once per claim on only that claim and the final answer; the original task prompt is absent from the reproduced v3 evaluator template. It maps fulfilled/partially fulfilled/not fulfilled to 1/0.5/0. Coverage is the mean claim score, and only coverage >= 0.75 passes. Pass rate is aggregated across N=1,000 tasks; its 95% CI uses 10,000 nonparametric bootstrap resamples and the 2.5th/97.5th percentiles. GPT-5.4 and Claude Opus 4.6 independently rescore all tasks only for cross-judge sensitivity (2.1-4.6 percentage-point ranges); they are not averaged into the primary leaderboard. The 11-mode diagnosis (four tool-call plus seven cognitive modes) runs only when coverage < 0.75 and never changes scoring. The v3 paper reports 20 models from six providers and a best Pass@0.75 of 82.2%. Public data was separately pinned to Hugging Face commit b5bcde2236c0b8772020e13dea4e481241e78677; MCP-Atlas.parquet is the LFS object with SHA-256 2d7bc052f14cbcb3b8294293481053f7111d256f9c9deaa96f3ff632d19958d0 and contains exactly 500 rows with TASK, ENABLED_TOOLS, PROMPT, GTFA_CLAIMS, and TRAJECTORY under CC BY 4.0. Direct parsing gives 7-37 enabled tools (mean 15.196; union 220), 2-8 distinct called tools in the reference trace (mean 4.110), 3-17 tool calls (mean 4.846), and 1-23 claims under the released scorer fallback (mean 3.904). This intentionally remains separate from full-set paper statistics. The HF card's 10-25 enabled-tools and 3-6 tool-call claims do not describe the pinned Parquet exactly: six rows fall outside 10-25 and 50 rows exceed six calls. Five ENABLED_TOOLS cells contain tool-definition objects while the other 495 contain name strings; one GTFA_CLAIMS value is not a valid JSON or Python list literal and relies on text fallback; serialized trajectories contain no explicit dependency field. The paper calls the reference trajectory a mean 9.8 tool-call steps, whereas the public file has 2,423 tool calls (4.846/task) and 4,852 assistant/tool messages (9.704/task), so the diagram labels 9.8 as the paper's step statistic and keeps measured calls separate. The public harness was audited at b6edd44b69892894ffa282f356e2dba41b41e298. At audit time, registry tag ghcr.io/scaleapi/mcp-atlas:1.2.7 resolved to OCI index digest sha256:24e6ed3534916afe2c6825382da159a30e23516ef612be5d074fd96a74f9184c; this is an evidentiary registry snapshot, not a runner-enforced pin. The public run_eval path passes the mutable 1.2.7 tag, the run_all path uses a locally retagged latest image, and the sandbox client accepts MCP_SANDBOX_URL without validating an image digest. Its 36-server catalog exposes 307 tools, while 220 is the task-enabled union; these are different scopes, not merged counts. The current runner fetches ScaleAI/MCP-Atlas without a revision pin. Paper/public-code gaps are explicit: the paper says harness/evaluator code is Apache-2.0, but the pinned repository LICENSE is MIT; the paper reports up to five retries per task with error summaries, but the public TypeScript v2 outer wrapper makes three attempts (at most two retries) for HTTP 500/502/503/429 and timeouts, while its LiteLLM adapter separately permits up to five retries (six attempts) for HTTP 401/429; neither mechanism is the paper-reported whole-task retry; Section 3.1 says servers restart between evaluation runs, the appendix says between tasks, and the public v2 loop disables sandbox reset while documenting a shareable sandbox. Upstream live APIs therefore remain a reproducibility bound even with container pins. Finally, the live Scale Labs page is a mutable result surface: its April 2026 methodology states Gemini 2.5 Pro, includes the original task prompt, adds transient-error retry handling, and uses a 100-call budget, while v3 uses Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview with claim-plus-answer-only input as primary and the current page contains model rows beyond the paper. Live scores are therefore not used as paper-v3 construction evidence.
